The Two Faces of a Wage: One Firm vs the Whole Economy

In micro, a wage is a cost the firm pays. In macro, that same wage is also the household's income.

One firm that cuts wages can hire more people. But what if every firm cuts at once? Customers' wallets get thinner, and goods stop selling. In the end, the jobs themselves vanish. The formula below traces that chain.

For example, a corner 🏪 bakery that cuts 💵 pay can afford one more helper. But if every shop in town cuts pay, customers have less to spend and 🍞 bread stops selling. Then helper jobs disappear too.

L=60−4wL = 60 - 4wL=60−4w
ΔY=c⋅ΔB1−c\Delta Y = \frac{c \cdot \Delta B}{1 - c}ΔY=1−cc⋅ΔB​

Examples & Exercises

One cafe cuts its wage from 101010 to 888 (labor demand L=60−4wL = 60 - 4wL=60−4w, each worker brings in sales of 141414).

What happens to its jobs and profit?

Show proof

  1. Slide down the demand curve: at wage 101010, L=60−4⋅10=20L = 60 - 4 \cdot 10 = 20L=60−4⋅10=20 workers; at wage 888, L=60−4⋅8=28L = 60 - 4 \cdot 8 = 28L=60−4⋅8=28. Jobs rise by 888.

  2. Profit is the per-worker margin (14−w)(14 - w)(14−w) times jobs: before, (14−10)⋅20=80(14 - 10) \cdot 20 = 80(14−10)⋅20=80; after, (14−8)⋅28=168(14 - 8) \cdot 28 = 168(14−8)⋅28=168.

    Costs down, headcount up, profit more than doubled.

    But the whole calculation stands on one assumption — that customers' incomes stay put. The next problem removes it.

Now every cafe in the country cuts wages by 222 at the same time.

In an economy with 100100100 workers, output per worker 151515, and MPC c=0.75c = 0.75c=0.75, what happens to jobs?

Show proof

  1. First, income leaks out: 100100100 workers each earning 222 less shrinks the wage bill by 200200200, and consumption falls by 0.750.750.75 of that, 150150150. The multiplier 11−0.75=4\frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 41−0.751​=4 amplifies it: output falls by 150⋅4=600150 \cdot 4 = 600150⋅4=600, from 150015001500 to 900900900.

  2. Jobs are output divided by output per worker: 900/15=60900 / 15 = 60900/15=60. Wages were cut, yet 404040 jobs vanished.

    The wage bill did not stop at the intended 200200200 drop either — with wages and jobs falling together it lands at 8⋅60=4808 \cdot 60 = 4808⋅60=480, a fall of 520520520.

    The prescription that worked for one firm works in reverse for the whole: the fallacy of composition.
